concepts.def: Reproduction by a single parent without meiosis or the fusion of gametes, so that the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and to each other (clones). Its relative advantage is that an individual already adapted to an existing, stable environment passes on the whole of its successful genotype to every offspring, and reproduction can be rapid because no mate is needed.

Reproduction in which two gametes, produced by meiosis, fuse to form a zygote. The offspring carry new combinations of alleles, so a population reproducing sexually shows the genetic variation on which natural selection can act; its relative advantage is that some offspring are likely to be adapted to a changed environment. Its costs are that it takes longer, requires a mate, and breaks up the parent's own successful allele combination.

concepts.term: Meiosis in the sexual life cycle
concepts.def: The nuclear division that halves the chromosome number to produce haploid gametes. Because homologous chromosomes are separated at random (independent assortment) and exchange segments by crossing over, meiosis breaks up the parental combinations of alleles: no gamete carries the same allele combination as the parent's body cells.

The fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete to form a diploid zygote. Fertilization restores the diploid number and, because any male gamete may fuse with any female gamete, it produces new combinations of alleles that neither parent possessed. Fusion of gametes and fertilization are the same event.

A haploid sex cell produced by meiosis. In animals the male gamete is a sperm and the female gamete an egg; in flowering plants the male gametes develop inside pollen grains and the female gamete inside an ovule. Two gametes fuse at fertilization to form a diploid zygote.

The gamete that travels to the female gamete. Because it must move, it is small and motile with very little stored food, and it can be produced in very large numbers at low cost to the parent. In humans the male gamete is a sperm, with a flagellum for swimming and many mitochondria to supply ATP for movement.

The gamete that stays in place and is reached by the male gamete. It is large and non-motile, with food reserves in its cytoplasm to support the early embryo, so it is costly to make and is produced in far smaller numbers than male gametes. In humans the female gamete is the egg, which is released one at a time at ovulation.

The pattern of investment a sex makes in producing gametes and in its offspring. Because male gametes are small, cheap and numerous, a male can potentially father very many offspring and typically competes for mates; because female gametes are large, costly and few, a female's reproductive success is limited by the number of eggs she can make and provision, so females typically invest more in each offspring and are more selective in mating.

The male gonad, held in the scrotum outside the body cavity where the slightly lower temperature favours sperm production. The testes produce sperm by meiosis in the seminiferous tubules and secrete the hormone testosterone.
A long coiled tube on the surface of each testis in which sperm produced in the testis mature and are stored until ejaculation.
The muscular tube that carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra during ejaculation, passing the seminal vesicle and prostate gland on the way.

Accessory glands that add fluid to the sperm to form semen. The seminal vesicles secrete an alkaline fluid containing fructose, which the sperm respire for ATP; the prostate gland secretes an alkaline fluid that neutralizes the acidity of the vagina. Neither gland makes or stores sperm.
The tube running through the penis that carries semen out of the body during ejaculation and urine out of the body from the bladder at other times; the two never pass at the same time.

The female gonad. Each ovary contains follicles in which eggs develop and mature; one follicle bursts at ovulation each cycle to release an egg. The ovary also secretes the hormones oestradiol (from developing follicles) and progesterone (from the corpus luteum).

The tube leading from near each ovary to the uterus. Its funnel-shaped opening collects the egg released at ovulation, ciliated cells move the egg towards the uterus, and it is the site where fertilization normally takes place.

The uterus is the muscular organ in which the embryo implants and the foetus develops. Its inner lining, the endometrium, thickens and becomes rich in blood vessels during each uterine cycle in readiness for implantation, and is shed at menstruation if no embryo implants.

The cervix is the narrow neck of the uterus that opens into the vagina; it produces mucus and dilates during childbirth. The vagina is the muscular tube leading from the cervix to the outside of the body; it receives the penis and semen during sexual intercourse and is the birth canal.

The roughly 28-day cycle of changes in the ovary (ovarian cycle) and in the endometrium of the uterus (uterine cycle), which together constitute the menstrual cycle. It is regulated by FSH and LH from the pituitary gland and by oestradiol and progesterone from the ovary, through both negative and positive feedback.

The sequence of events in the ovary: FSH stimulates a group of follicles to develop, one dominant follicle matures and secretes oestradiol (follicular phase), a surge of LH causes it to burst and release its egg (ovulation, around day 14), and the remains of the follicle form the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (luteal phase) before degenerating if no pregnancy occurs.

The sequence of changes in the endometrium: it is shed during menstruation (days 1 to about 5), rebuilt and thickened under the influence of oestradiol, and maintained and further thickened with a rich blood supply under progesterone from the corpus luteum. When the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls, the endometrium breaks down and the next menstruation begins.

A hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland at the start of the cycle. It stimulates the development of follicles in the ovary and stimulates the developing follicles to secrete oestradiol. Its secretion is inhibited by negative feedback from progesterone and by low levels of oestradiol.

A hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. A sharp surge of LH, triggered by positive feedback from the high level of oestradiol from the mature follicle, causes ovulation and then stimulates the ruptured follicle to become the corpus luteum.

A steroid hormone secreted by the developing follicles in the ovary. It stimulates the endometrium to thicken after menstruation, and its rising level in the days before ovulation acts by positive feedback on the pituitary to trigger the surge of LH (and a smaller rise in FSH) that causes ovulation. At low levels, together with progesterone, it inhibits FSH and LH secretion by negative feedback.

A steroid hormone secreted by the corpus luteum after ovulation (and by the placenta during pregnancy). It maintains and further thickens the endometrium and, by negative feedback on the pituitary, inhibits FSH and LH secretion so that no further follicles develop during the luteal phase. When the corpus luteum degenerates the fall in progesterone causes menstruation.

The yellow body formed from the wall of the follicle after ovulation, under the influence of LH. It secretes progesterone (and some oestradiol) for about ten days. If no embryo implants it degenerates, hormone levels fall and menstruation follows; if pregnancy occurs it is maintained by hCG from the embryo.

concepts.term: Positive and negative feedback in the menstrual cycle
concepts.def: Negative feedback: progesterone and low-level oestradiol inhibit the pituitary's secretion of FSH and LH, holding the cycle in check during the luteal phase. Positive feedback: the rising oestradiol from the mature follicle stimulates the pituitary to secrete more LH (and FSH), which stimulates more oestradiol secretion, so LH rises steeply to the surge that causes ovulation.

The event in human fertilization in which the cell membrane of the sperm fuses with the cell membrane of the egg. Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg cytoplasm; the sperm's tail (flagellum) and its mitochondria are destroyed, so all the mitochondria of the zygote come from the egg.

After the sperm nucleus has entered the egg, the nuclear membranes of the sperm nucleus and the egg nucleus dissolve, and all the condensed chromosomes from both nuclei line up together on a single spindle in a joint mitosis. The result is two diploid nuclei, one in each of the first two cells of the embryo; the two haploid nuclei do not first fuse into a single diploid nucleus.

A fertility treatment in which eggs are collected from the ovaries and fertilized with sperm outside the body (in vitro means in glass), and one or more of the resulting embryos are transferred to the uterus. Hormone treatment is used first to suspend the woman's own cycle and then to induce superovulation.

The maturation and release of many eggs in a single cycle, induced in IVF by injecting artificial doses of FSH (with LH or hCG to trigger final maturation) after the normal secretion of pituitary hormones has been suspended with a drug. It allows several eggs to be collected at once so that several embryos can be produced.

The structure inside the ovary of a flower in which the female gamete is produced by meiosis followed by mitosis. After fertilization the ovule develops into a seed containing the embryo, and the ovary around it develops into the fruit.

The structure produced in the anther, by meiosis followed by mitosis, that contains the male gametes of a flowering plant. The pollen grain is not itself a gamete: it carries the gamete nuclei to the stigma and, on germinating, grows a pollen tube that delivers them to the ovule.

The transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma. Pollination is not fertilization: it is followed by pollen development (growth of a pollen tube down the style) and only then by the fusion of a male gamete with the female gamete inside the ovule.

The tube that grows from a germinating pollen grain on the stigma, down through the style to an ovule, carrying the male gametes. When it reaches the ovule a male gamete fuses with the female gamete (fertilization) to produce a zygote, which develops into the embryo of the seed.

A plant whose flowers produce both male gametes (in pollen) and female gametes (in ovules). Its reproduction is still sexual, because gametes are produced by meiosis and fuse at fertilization, even when a flower fertilizes itself; the offspring may differ genetically from the parent if it is heterozygous, and in any case are produced by meiosis and fertilization rather than by mitosis alone.

The male part of a flower. The anther produces pollen grains, containing the male gametes, and releases them when ripe; the filament is the stalk that holds the anther in a position where visiting insects brush against it.

The female part of a flower. The stigma is the sticky surface that receives pollen grains; the style is the stalk through which pollen tubes grow; the ovary contains the ovules, in which the female gametes are produced and which become seeds after fertilization.

In an insect-pollinated flower the petals are large and brightly coloured, often scented and marked, to attract insects; the nectary at the base of the flower secretes sugary nectar as a reward, positioned so that an insect feeding on it touches the anthers and stigma.
One of the outer, usually green, leaf-like parts of a flower that enclose and protect the flower while it is a bud.

The transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower on one plant to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. It brings together gametes from two parents and so increases genetic variation in the offspring. Pollen is carried between plants by animals (mainly insects) or by wind.
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant. The gametes come from one parent, so the offspring are less varied and inbreeding results.

Features that make self-pollination unlikely: the anthers and stigma of a flower maturing at different times, so a flower's own pollen is shed before or after its stigma is receptive; separate male and female flowers on the same plant (monoecious species); male and female flowers on separate plants (dioecious species); and reliance on animals or wind to carry pollen from plant to plant.

A genetic mechanism in many plant species that prevents a plant's own pollen (or pollen from a genetically similar plant) from fertilizing its eggs, for example by stopping the pollen tube growing down the style when the pollen and the carpel carry matching alleles of the self-incompatibility gene. It ensures that the gametes fusing at fertilization come from different plants, increasing genetic variation within the species.

Breeding between closely related individuals, of which self-pollination is the extreme case. It decreases genetic diversity in the population and, by increasing the proportion of offspring homozygous for harmful recessive alleles, reduces vigour (inbreeding depression).

The transport of seeds away from the parent plant, for example by wind, water or animals that eat fruits or carry hooked seeds. It is distinct from pollination, which is the transfer of pollen and happens before fertilization; dispersal happens after fertilization and reduces competition between the parent and its offspring.

The growth and development of the embryo in a seed into a seedling. The seed absorbs water, the embryo produces gibberellin which stimulates the mobilization of food reserves, the radicle (embryonic root) emerges and then the shoot, until the seedling's leaves can photosynthesize.

The conversion of the insoluble food stores of a seed, such as starch, into soluble substances that can be transported to the growing embryo and respired: in germinating cereal grains, amylase is synthesized in response to gibberellin and hydrolyses starch to maltose, which is converted to glucose for cell respiration and growth.

A hormone secreted by the hypothalamus that stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to release the gonadotropins LH and FSH. Increased GnRH release towards the end of childhood triggers the increase in LH and FSH secretion that starts puberty.

The period of developmental change during which the reproductive system becomes functional. It begins when the hypothalamus increases its release of GnRH, which raises LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the testes to secrete testosterone or the ovaries to secrete oestradiol and progesterone, and the increased steroid sex hormones cause the physical changes associated with puberty.

The production of sperm in the seminiferous tubules of the testes from puberty onwards. Cells in the outer layer of the tubule divide by mitosis to maintain their numbers, some grow slightly, then each undergoes the two divisions of meiosis to give four haploid cells of equal size, which differentiate into sperm. Millions of sperm are produced each day throughout adult life.

The production of eggs in the ovaries. Before birth, cells divide by mitosis, grow, and begin meiosis but stop early in the first division. From puberty, each cycle a few of these cells resume meiosis: the first division is unequal, giving a large secondary oocyte and a small polar body; the secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and completes the second division, again unequally, only if a sperm enters it. One functional egg with a large cytoplasm results, and only a few hundred are ever released.

A tiny cell produced by the unequal cytoplasmic division at each meiotic division of oogenesis. It receives a haploid set of chromosomes but almost no cytoplasm, and degenerates; this is how one cell entering meiosis gives a single egg that keeps nearly all the cytoplasm and food reserves.

The release of hydrolytic enzymes from the acrosome, a membrane-bound vesicle in the head of the sperm, when the sperm contacts the zona pellucida. The enzymes digest a path through the zona pellucida so that the sperm can reach and fuse with the egg cell membrane.

The release, by exocytosis, of the contents of cortical granules from the egg cytoplasm into the space around the egg as soon as a sperm's membrane fuses with the egg membrane. The enzymes released alter the zona pellucida so that it hardens and no longer binds sperm, preventing any further sperm from passing through and so preventing polyspermy.

The glycoprotein coat surrounding the egg cell membrane. A sperm must digest its way through it (acrosome reaction) to fuse with the egg; after fertilization the cortical reaction changes it into a barrier that blocks all other sperm.

The entry of more than one sperm nucleus into an egg. It would give a zygote with too many sets of chromosomes, which cannot develop normally, so it is prevented by the cortical reaction that follows entry of the first sperm.

The stage of the human embryo, reached about five to seven days after fertilization by repeated mitotic divisions while it is moved down the oviduct to the uterus. It is a hollow ball of cells with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that will form the foetus, and an outer layer of cells that attaches to the endometrium at implantation and later contributes to the placenta.

The attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium and its sinking into the lining, about seven days after fertilization. The outer cells of the blastocyst begin to secrete hCG and to draw nutrients from the endometrium, and the embryo can then continue its development inside the uterus.

A hormone secreted by the embryo, from its outer cells at implantation, and then by the developing placenta. It maintains the corpus luteum so that progesterone secretion continues and the endometrium is not shed. Because it is made only by an embryo, its presence in the mother's urine is the basis of pregnancy testing.

An antibody produced by a single clone of identical cells, so every molecule binds the same specific antigen. Pregnancy tests use monoclonal antibodies that bind hCG: one, attached to a coloured marker, binds hCG in urine as it flows along the test strip, and a second, fixed in a line on the strip, captures the hCG-antibody complexes so that a coloured line appears only when hCG is present.

The disc-shaped organ formed from foetal tissue and the endometrium through which the foetus exchanges substances with the mother. Oxygen, glucose, amino acids, lipids, water, vitamins, minerals and antibodies pass from maternal to foetal blood, and carbon dioxide, urea and other wastes pass the other way, without the two bloods mixing. By providing for the foetus in this way it allows the foetus to be retained in the uterus to a much later stage of development than in mammals without a placenta; it also secretes progesterone and oestradiol.

Finger-like projections of foetal tissue, containing foetal capillaries, that extend into pools of maternal blood in the placenta. Their very large total surface area, and the short distance between maternal blood and foetal capillaries, allow rapid exchange of materials by diffusion and active transport.

Pregnancy continues only while progesterone levels remain high: progesterone maintains the endometrium and inhibits contractions of the uterine muscle. In the first weeks the progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum, kept alive by hCG from the embryo; by about the end of the first trimester the placenta has taken over progesterone (and oestradiol) secretion and the corpus luteum degenerates.

A hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary gland that stimulates contraction of the uterine muscle during childbirth. At the end of pregnancy a fall in progesterone removes the inhibition of contractions; each contraction stretches the cervix, stretch receptors signal to the pituitary and more oxytocin is secreted, causing stronger contractions. This positive feedback continues until the baby is delivered.

Treatment of women during and after the menopause with oestrogen (with or without progesterone) to replace the hormones the ovaries no longer secrete, relieving menopausal symptoms. Early epidemiological studies reported that women on HRT had a lower incidence of coronary heart disease, but later randomized controlled trials showed that HRT causes a small increase in CHD risk.

An observational study that looks for correlations between a factor (such as taking HRT) and a health outcome (such as coronary heart disease) across a population, without the researchers controlling who is exposed. Because the groups being compared may differ in other ways (confounding variables), a correlation found in such a study cannot by itself establish cause and effect.

An experiment in which participants are allocated at random to receive the treatment or a placebo, so that confounding variables such as socioeconomic status are spread evenly between the groups. It can test cause and effect: randomized controlled trials of HRT showed that HRT slightly increases the risk of CHD, overturning the conclusion drawn from the earlier correlation.

mcqs.q: What is the relative advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
options: Its offspring carry new gene combinations, giving the variation needed for a changed environment.
Its offspring gain the particular features that a changed environment comes to require.
Its offspring are better adapted than the parent in every environment, so more of them survive.
Its offspring carry new alleles produced by meiosis, which asexual offspring cannot receive.
mcqs.specStatementText: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
mcqs.explain: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, so among them some are likely to be adapted to an environment that has changed. This is its relative advantage; asexual reproduction's is the faithful copying of a genotype already adapted to the existing environment.
rationales: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, so among them some are likely to be adapted to an environment that has changed. This is its relative advantage; asexual reproduction's is the faithful copying of a genotype already adapted to the existing environment.
A student who thinks variation is produced to meet a need picks this. Meiosis and fertilization generate new combinations blindly; the environment selects among them afterwards.
A student who believes sexual reproduction is always superior picks this. In a stable environment a well-adapted parent does better to copy its genotype asexually than to break it up.
A student who thinks meiosis makes new alleles picks this. New alleles arise only by mutation, in asexual lineages too; meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of existing alleles.

mcqs.q: Aphids reproduce asexually through the summer, when conditions are stable and food is plentiful, and switch to sexual reproduction in autumn before conditions change. Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: Sexual reproduction is used in autumn because varied offspring are invariably fitter; the summer clones are a poor substitute produced under time pressure.
Summer clones copy an adapted genotype quickly; autumn sexual reproduction produces varied offspring for the changed conditions ahead.
Sexual reproduction is used in autumn so that the offspring gain the specific cold-tolerance features that the coming winter demands.
Asexual reproduction in summer shows that aphids are simple organisms; the autumn sexual stage is their true form of reproduction.
mcqs.specStatementText: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
mcqs.explain: Asexual reproduction suits an individual already adapted to the existing environment, giving many identical offspring fast. Sexual reproduction produces new gene combinations, the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment.
rationales: A student who believes variation is always an advantage picks this. In stable summer conditions the clones are the better strategy: every offspring inherits the whole adapted genotype.

Asexual reproduction suits an individual already adapted to the existing environment, giving many identical offspring fast. Sexual reproduction produces new gene combinations, the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment.
A student who thinks variation is directed towards what is needed picks this. New allele combinations are random; some may happen to suit winter, and selection then favours those.

A student who files asexual reproduction with bacteria and simple organisms picks this. Many eukaryotes, including these insects, use both modes; the choice depends on the environment, not on complexity.

mcqs.q: In the sexual life cycle, what are the respective roles of meiosis and fusion of gametes in producing genetic variation?
options: Meiosis produces new alleles by mutation, and fusion of gametes combines the alleles of the two parents.
Meiosis is the only source of variation, and fusion of gametes merely restores the diploid number.
Meiosis breaks up parental allele combinations, and fusion of gametes produces new combinations.
Meiosis halves the parental allele set but keeps it intact, and fusion of gametes restores it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis breaks up combinations; fertilization makes new ones
mcqs.explain: This is the guide's statement of the two roles: meiosis breaks up parental combinations of alleles, and fusion of gametes (fertilization) produces new combinations.
rationales: A student who merges mutation with meiosis picks this. Meiosis does not make alleles; it separates and reshuffles the alleles the parent already has.
A student who treats fertilization as a mechanical ending picks this. Because any sperm may fuse with any egg, fusion of gametes is itself a source of new combinations.
This is the guide's statement of the two roles: meiosis breaks up parental combinations of alleles, and fusion of gametes (fertilization) produces new combinations.
A student who pictures a gamete as half a copy of the parent picks this. Independent assortment and crossing over mean no gamete carries the parent's own combination intact.

mcqs.q: Two full siblings have the same two parents yet differ in many of their alleles. Which explanation is correct?
options: Each parent passed on the same half of its alleles both times, but the halves combined differently in each child.
New alleles arose by mutation during the meiosis that produced the gametes for each sibling.
Meiosis alone made the gametes differ; which sperm met which egg made no difference to the alleles.
Each gamete carried a different selection of parental alleles, and different gametes fused.
mcqs.specStatementText: Meiosis breaks up combinations; fertilization makes new ones
mcqs.explain: Meiosis broke up each parent's allele combination differently in each gamete, and fertilization brought together a different pair of gametes for each child, producing two new combinations.
rationales: A student who thinks a parent hands over a fixed half picks this. Meiosis gives every gamete a different selection of alleles, so the halves themselves differed.
A student who credits meiosis with making alleles picks this. Mutation is rare; the siblings differ because existing alleles were shuffled into different combinations.
A student who denies fertilization any role picks this. Which of the many varied sperm fused with which egg determined each sibling's combination, so fusion of gametes contributed too.
Meiosis broke up each parent's allele combination differently in each gamete, and fertilization brought together a different pair of gametes for each child, producing two new combinations.

mcqs.q: In a fish species the female lays a few hundred large eggs in a nest and the male releases many millions of tiny sperm over them. Which statement explains the difference in size and number?
options: Sperm must travel to the eggs, so they are small with few food reserves and can be produced cheaply in vast numbers.
Eggs are larger because each one carries far more of the genetic material than a sperm does.
The numbers should be equal since one sperm fertilizes one egg; the surplus sperm are defective ones.
Sperm are small because so many are made that only a little cytoplasm is available for each one.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why sperm are small and many, eggs large and few
mcqs.explain: The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is smaller with less food reserves than the egg. From this follow the differences in numbers of gametes.
rationales: The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is smaller with less food reserves than the egg. From this follow the differences in numbers of gametes.
A student who equates cell size with DNA content picks this. Sperm and egg each contribute one haploid set; the egg's extra bulk is cytoplasm with food reserves.
A student who reasons back from one-to-one fertilization picks this. Vast numbers of normal sperm are released because only a tiny fraction complete the journey to an egg.
A student who reverses the cause picks this. Sperm are small because they must travel; being small and cheap is what makes it possible to produce so many.

mcqs.q: A student annotates a diagram of the male reproductive system. Which annotation is correct?
options: Urethra: carries urine only, because semen leaves through a separate duct in the penis.
Epididymis: stores sperm while they mature after their production in the testis.
Seminal vesicle: stores the sperm until they are required for ejaculation.
Testis: produces the semen that carries sperm along the duct to the urethra.
mcqs.specStatementText: The human reproductive systems, part by part
mcqs.explain: Sperm are produced in the testis and pass into the epididymis, the coiled tube on its surface, where they mature and are stored until ejaculation.
rationales: A student who knows the urethra only from the excretory system picks this. The sperm duct joins the urethra, which carries semen during ejaculation and urine at other times.
Sperm are produced in the testis and pass into the epididymis, the coiled tube on its surface, where they mature and are stored until ejaculation.
A student misled by the name picks this. The seminal vesicles are glands that add alkaline, fructose-containing fluid to sperm; they do not store them.
A student who equates semen with sperm picks this. The testis produces sperm; the fluid of semen is added by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.

mcqs.q: A student annotates a diagram of the female reproductive system. Which annotation is correct?
options: Uterus: the site of fertilization and, later, of implantation of the embryo.
Endometrium: the thick muscular wall of the uterus that contracts during childbirth.
Oviduct: the site of fertilization; it moves the egg towards the uterus.
Ovary: releases an egg into the oviduct on day 1 of each menstruation.
mcqs.specStatementText: The human reproductive systems, part by part
mcqs.explain: The oviduct collects the egg released at ovulation, its cilia move the egg towards the uterus, and it is where sperm normally meet and fertilize the egg.
rationales: A student who places every reproductive event in the uterus picks this. Fertilization occurs in the oviduct; only implantation occurs in the uterus.
A student who confuses the lining with the wall picks this. The endometrium is the inner lining that thickens each cycle and is shed at menstruation.
The oviduct collects the egg released at ovulation, its cilia move the egg towards the uterus, and it is where sperm normally meet and fertilize the egg.
A student who ties the egg's release to the visible bleeding picks this. Ovulation happens around day 14, not at the start of menstruation.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the feedback control operating in the days just before ovulation?
options: High oestradiol inhibits LH secretion by negative feedback, as in the rest of the cycle.
Progesterone secreted by the pituitary stimulates oestradiol release by positive feedback.
High oestradiol stimulates FSH secretion, and it is the FSH that then causes ovulation.
High oestradiol stimulates LH secretion by positive feedback on the pituitary.
mcqs.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
mcqs.explain: Rising oestradiol from the maturing follicle stimulates the pituitary to release more LH, which stimulates more oestradiol: positive feedback that produces the LH surge and ovulation.
rationales: A student who has only met negative feedback picks this. Before ovulation the high oestradiol from the mature follicle stimulates LH release, which is positive feedback.
A student who puts every cycle hormone in the pituitary picks this. Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum, which does not exist until after ovulation.
A student who attributes ovulation to FSH picks this. FSH does rise slightly, but the LH surge is what causes the follicle to burst.
Rising oestradiol from the maturing follicle stimulates the pituitary to release more LH, which stimulates more oestradiol: positive feedback that produces the LH surge and ovulation.

mcqs.q: Blood samples were taken from a woman on day 7 and day 21 of a regular 28-day cycle. Progesterone was very low on day 7 and high on day 21. What can be concluded about day 21?
options: A corpus luteum has formed after ovulation and is secreting progesterone that maintains the endometrium.
The pituitary gland has increased its progesterone output in preparation for menstruation.
Ovulation is about to occur, because the egg is released when menstruation begins on day 28.
The rising progesterone will itself trigger the menstruation that is due on day 28.
mcqs.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
mcqs.explain: High progesterone a week after mid-cycle shows that ovulation has occurred and the ruptured follicle has become a corpus luteum, whose progesterone keeps the thickened endometrium in place.
rationales: High progesterone a week after mid-cycle shows that ovulation has occurred and the ruptured follicle has become a corpus luteum, whose progesterone keeps the thickened endometrium in place.
A student who assigns progesterone to the pituitary picks this. Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum in the ovary, and it postpones menstruation rather than preparing for it.
A student who links egg release to menstruation picks this. Ovulation occurred around day 14; the high progesterone is evidence that it has already happened.
A student who expects a rise to cause the event picks this. Menstruation follows the fall in progesterone when the corpus luteum degenerates.

mcqs.q: What is the role of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in the ovarian cycle?
options: It causes the mature follicle to burst and release its egg at ovulation.
It stimulates the follicles to develop and to secrete oestradiol.
It is made in the corpus luteum to maintain the endometrium.
Its rise at the end of the cycle is what triggers menstruation.
mcqs.specStatementText: The menstrual cycle and its hormones
mcqs.explain: FSH from the pituitary stimulates a group of follicles to develop at the start of the cycle and stimulates the developing follicles to secrete oestradiol.
rationales: A student who reads 'follicle-stimulating' as doing everything to the follicle picks this. Ovulation is caused by the surge of LH.
FSH from the pituitary stimulates a group of follicles to develop at the start of the cycle and stimulates the developing follicles to secrete oestradiol.
A student who has muddled which gland makes which hormone picks this. FSH is a pituitary hormone; the corpus luteum secretes progesterone.
A student who looks for a rising hormone to explain menstruation picks this. FSH does rise as progesterone falls, but it is the fall in progesterone that causes the endometrium to break down.

mcqs.q: Which event occurs during fertilization in humans?
options: The whole sperm enters the egg, so the embryo inherits its mitochondria from both parents.
The sperm and egg nuclei fuse into a single diploid nucleus before any cell division occurs.
The sperm nucleus enters the egg but the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
Enzymes from the sperm digest a hole in the egg membrane to let the nucleus in.
mcqs.specStatementText: What happens at fertilization in humans
mcqs.explain: After the sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane, the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the tail and mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote.
rationales: A student who pictures the sperm entering as a complete cell picks this. Only the nucleus enters; the tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
A student who learned 'the nuclei fuse' at GCSE picks this. The nuclear membranes dissolve and the chromosomes join a mitosis that directly produces two diploid nuclei.
After the sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane, the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the tail and mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote.
A student who extends the acrosome enzymes to the egg membrane picks this. Entry is by fusion of the two cell membranes; enzymes act only on the coat outside the membrane.

mcqs.q: A mutation in mitochondrial DNA is passed from a mother to all her children but is never passed on by a father. Which feature of fertilization explains this?
options: Sperm mitochondria enter the egg but are so outnumbered by the egg's own that their DNA is diluted away.
Each parent hands over exactly half of its DNA, and the mitochondrial DNA happens to fall in the mother's half.
The egg is larger because it carries more genetic material, including all the mitochondria required.
The sperm's mitochondria are destroyed after its nucleus has entered the egg cytoplasm.
mcqs.specStatementText: What happens at fertilization in humans
mcqs.explain: Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed. All the zygote's mitochondria, and so all its mitochondrial DNA, come from the egg.
rationales: A student who believes the sperm's mitochondria get in picks this. They do not enter: they are destroyed with the tail, so no paternal mitochondrial DNA is present to be diluted.

A student who pictures inheritance as each parent handing over a fixed half of its DNA picks this. Meiosis halves the nuclear DNA only; mitochondrial DNA is not part of that division, and the father passes on none because the sperm's mitochondria are destroyed at fertilization.

A student who equates the egg's size with extra genetic material picks this. The egg's size is due to food reserves; maternal inheritance of mitochondria is due to the fate of the sperm's mitochondria.
Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed. All the zygote's mitochondria, and so all its mitochondrial DNA, come from the egg.

mcqs.q: IVF treatment begins with a drug that suspends the woman's own secretion of FSH and LH, followed by daily injections of FSH. Why is this done?
options: Suspending her own cycle stops it interfering, so injected FSH can induce superovulation and many eggs be collected.
The injected FSH strengthens her natural cycle so that one egg is released at a predictable time.
The injections make fertilization possible in the oviduct once sperm are introduced into the body.
The FSH injections cause ovulation, so that the released eggs can be collected from the uterus.
mcqs.specStatementText: Hormones in IVF
mcqs.explain: The normal secretion of hormones is suspended so the natural cycle does not interfere; artificial doses of FSH then stimulate many follicles to develop at once (superovulation), giving several eggs for collection.
rationales: The normal secretion of hormones is suspended so the natural cycle does not interfere; artificial doses of FSH then stimulate many follicles to develop at once (superovulation), giving several eggs for collection.
A student who thinks IVF works within the normal cycle picks this. The aim is many eggs, not one, and the natural cycle has been deliberately switched off.
A student who confuses IVF with artificial insemination picks this. In IVF fertilization takes place outside the body, in the laboratory.
A student who attributes ovulation to FSH picks this. FSH stimulates follicle development; eggs are collected from the follicles before ovulation occurs.

mcqs.q: Where are the gametes of a flowering plant produced?
options: The pollen grains themselves are the male gametes and the ovules are the female gametes.
Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes inside ovules.
Male gametes are produced in the stigma and female gametes in the anther.
Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes in the seeds.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
mcqs.explain: Gametes are produced inside ovules (female, within the ovary) and inside pollen grains (male, within the anther); pollination and pollen tube growth bring them together.
rationales: A student who casts pollen as the plant's sperm picks this. Pollen grains and ovules are structures inside which the gametes are produced.
Gametes are produced inside ovules (female, within the ovary) and inside pollen grains (male, within the anther); pollination and pollen tube growth bring them together.
A student who has swapped the two central structures picks this. The anther produces pollen (male); the stigma receives it and belongs to the female carpel.
A student who backdates seeds to the flower picks this. The ovary contains ovules; an ovule becomes a seed only after its gamete has been fertilized.

mcqs.q: Garden pea flowers pollinate and fertilize themselves before they open. Which statement about reproduction in the pea is correct?
options: It is asexual, because only one parent plant takes part in the process.
Fertilization is complete as soon as the pollen has landed on the flower's stigma.
It is sexual, because meiosis makes the gametes and they fuse at fertilization.
The pollen grains, being the male gametes, fuse directly with the ovules in the ovary.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
mcqs.explain: Reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant is hermaphroditic: gametes formed by meiosis fuse to give a zygote. Whether the offspring differ from the parent depends on how heterozygous it is; what makes the process sexual is meiosis and fusion of gametes, not the number of parents.
rationales: A student who defines asexual reproduction by the number of parents picks this. The pea's gametes are made by meiosis and fuse, so its reproduction is sexual even though it self-fertilizes.
A student who equates pollination with fertilization picks this. After pollination a pollen tube must grow down the style before a male gamete can fuse with the female gamete.

Reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant is hermaphroditic: gametes formed by meiosis fuse to give a zygote. Whether the offspring differ from the parent depends on how heterozygous it is; what makes the process sexual is meiosis and fusion of gametes, not the number of parents.
A student who treats pollen as the gamete picks this. The pollen grain grows a tube that delivers the male gametes it contains to the female gamete inside the ovule.

mcqs.q: Which structure of an insect-pollinated flower is correctly paired with its function?
options: Stigma: produces pollen grains and sheds them onto the bodies of visiting insects.
Ovary: holds the seeds until the fruit ripens and the seeds are dispersed.
Petal: brightly coloured to attract insects that carry the seeds away from the plant.
Stigma: sticky surface on which pollen grains land and then germinate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Parts of an insect-pollinated flower
mcqs.explain: The stigma is the receptive tip of the carpel; its sticky surface traps pollen brushed off a visiting insect, and the pollen tube then grows down the style.
rationales: A student who has swapped stigma and anther picks this. The anther produces and releases pollen; the stigma receives it.
A student who thinks the flower already contains seeds picks this. The ovary contains ovules, which become seeds only after fertilization.
A student who merges pollination with seed dispersal picks this. Petals attract insects that transfer pollen; seed dispersal happens later, after fertilization.
The stigma is the receptive tip of the carpel; its sticky surface traps pollen brushed off a visiting insect, and the pollen tube then grows down the style.

mcqs.q: In one flower species the anthers shed their pollen and wither several days before the stigma of the same flower becomes receptive. How does this promote cross-pollination?
options: The flower's own pollen is gone when its stigma is receptive, so only pollen brought from another plant can pollinate it.
It does not; a flower that has both stamens and carpels will pollinate itself whatever the timing of the two.
It ensures the pollen reaches other flowers on the same plant, which is precisely what cross-pollination means.
It provides the physical barrier that self-incompatibility genes require to keep pollen off the stigma.
mcqs.specStatementText: How plants avoid pollinating themselves
mcqs.explain: Different maturation times for pollen and stigma are a method of promoting cross-pollination: a flower cannot pollinate itself if its pollen is shed before its stigma can receive pollen.
rationales: Different maturation times for pollen and stigma are a method of promoting cross-pollination: a flower cannot pollinate itself if its pollen is shed before its stigma can receive pollen.
A student who reasons from the closeness of the parts picks this. Timing is exactly what stops the nearby pollen mattering: it is no longer there when the stigma is ready.
A student who thinks any flower-to-flower transfer is cross-pollination picks this. Transfer between flowers on one plant is still self-pollination; cross-pollination needs a different plant.
A student who thinks self-incompatibility is a physical block picks this. Self-incompatibility is a genetic recognition mechanism acting after pollen lands and is separate from timing.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a method that promotes cross-pollination?
options: Transfer of pollen between different flowers on the same plant.
Male and female flowers borne on separate individual plants.
Seeds carried away from the parent plant by animals.
The stigma physically rejecting its own flower's pollen.
mcqs.specStatementText: How plants avoid pollinating themselves
mcqs.explain: When a species has male and female flowers on different plants, pollen must be carried from one plant to another, so every pollination is a cross-pollination.
rationales: A student who counts any movement between flowers as crossing picks this. Pollen from the same plant carries the same genotype, so this is self-pollination.
When a species has male and female flowers on different plants, pollen must be carried from one plant to another, so every pollination is a cross-pollination.
A student who confuses dispersal with pollination picks this. Seed dispersal happens after fertilization and does not move pollen at all.
A student who thinks self-incompatibility is a physical barrier picks this. Self-incompatibility is genetic: the plant's own pollen may land, but its tube fails to grow.

mcqs.q: In a self-incompatible plant species, pollen from a flower lands on the stigma of the same flower and germinates, but no seed is set. Which statement about self-incompatibility explains this?
options: It works by physically preventing the flower's own pollen from ever landing on its stigma.
It prevents inbreeding, which would otherwise cause harmful new mutations in the offspring.
It stops a plant's own pollen from fertilizing its eggs, so preventing inbreeding.
It is needed because self-fertilization would be asexual and so produce clones.
mcqs.specStatementText: Self-incompatibility keeps gametes from different plants
mcqs.explain: Self-pollination leads to inbreeding, which decreases genetic diversity and vigour. Genetic self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants.
rationales: A student who models it on separate flowers and timing picks this. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism: matching alleles in pollen and carpel are recognized and the pollen tube is stopped.
A student who explains genetic defects by mutation picks this. Inbreeding makes harmful recessive alleles already present more likely to be homozygous; it creates no alleles.
Self-pollination leads to inbreeding, which decreases genetic diversity and vigour. Genetic self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants.
A student who thinks one parent means asexual picks this. Self-fertilization is still sexual reproduction; the problem is inbreeding, not cloning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between pollination and seed dispersal?
options: They are the same process: the wind or insect that carries the pollen also carries the seeds away.
Pollination is the fertilization of the flower; dispersal is the release of the fertilized pollen grains.
Pollination delivers pollen to the seeds already in the ovary; dispersal releases those seeds.
Pollination moves pollen to a stigma before fertilization; dispersal moves seeds after it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Seeds are dispersed, then germinate on stored food
mcqs.explain: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma and precedes fertilization. Seed dispersal is the movement of the seeds formed after fertilization away from the parent plant.
rationales: A student who sees the same agents in both lists picks this. Pollination happens before fertilization and moves pollen; dispersal happens after it and moves seeds.
A student who equates pollination with fertilization picks this. Pollination merely delivers pollen to the stigma, and what is dispersed is seeds, not pollen.
A student who thinks the flower already contains seeds picks this. The ovary holds ovules, which become seeds only after fertilization.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma and precedes fertilization. Seed dispersal is the movement of the seeds formed after fertilization away from the parent plant.

mcqs.q: A barley grain germinating in dark, moist soil grows a root and a shoot for several days. Where do the energy and materials for this growth come from?
options: Starch stored in the grain is hydrolysed by amylase to soluble sugars, which are moved to the embryo and respired.
The emerging shoot photosynthesizes using the small amount of light that reaches it through the soil.
The grain absorbs dissolved food from the surrounding soil along with the water that it takes up.
Water absorbed by the grain provides the mass, so the embryo grows by swelling rather than by respiring stores.
mcqs.specStatementText: Seeds are dispersed, then germinate on stored food
mcqs.explain: Germination involves the mobilization of food reserves: amylase, produced in response to gibberellin, hydrolyses starch to maltose, which is converted to glucose for cell respiration and growth of the embryo.
rationales: Germination involves the mobilization of food reserves: amylase, produced in response to gibberellin, hydrolyses starch to maltose, which is converted to glucose for cell respiration and growth of the embryo.
A student who links all plant growth to photosynthesis picks this. In darkness there is no photosynthesis; the seedling lives on its reserves until leaves reach the light.
A student who treats soil as food picks this. The soil supplies water and oxygen; the organic material comes from the seed's own stores.
A student who equates growth with swelling picks this. New cells and cell walls are built from the mobilized reserves using ATP from respiration; dry mass falls as the stores are used.

mcqs.q: A child whose hypothalamus cannot release GnRH fails to enter puberty, although the pituitary gland and gonads are normal. Which explanation is correct?
options: GnRH normally acts directly on the gonads, so without it they cannot make sex hormones; the pituitary gland plays no part in puberty.
Without GnRH the pituitary does not increase LH and FSH release, so the gonads are not stimulated to raise sex hormone production.
The gonads should start puberty on their own, so the fault must in fact lie in the testes or the ovaries themselves.
Puberty requires the pituitary gland to secrete the steroid sex hormones, which it cannot do without GnRH.
mcqs.specStatementText: Puberty starts in the hypothalamus
mcqs.explain: Puberty is triggered by increased GnRH release from the hypothalamus, which raises LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the gonads to secrete the sex hormones that cause the changes of puberty.
rationales: A student who reads 'gonadotropin' as 'acts on gonads' picks this. GnRH acts on the pituitary, which releases the gonadotropins LH and FSH that act on the gonads.

Puberty is triggered by increased GnRH release from the hypothalamus, which raises LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the gonads to secrete the sex hormones that cause the changes of puberty.
A student who places the origin of puberty in the gonads picks this. Normal gonads stay inactive without LH and FSH, which in turn depend on GnRH.
A student who thinks the pituitary makes steroid hormones picks this. The pituitary secretes LH and FSH; testosterone, oestradiol and progesterone are made by the gonads.

mcqs.q: Which comparison of spermatogenesis and oogenesis in humans is correct?
options: Each meiosis yields four gametes in both processes, but three of every four eggs degenerate before birth.
Both processes continue to produce new gametes from puberty right through to old age.
Each meiosis yields four sperm but only one egg, because oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally.
In both processes the two divisions of meiosis are completed inside the gonad before the gamete is released.
mcqs.specStatementText: Making sperm and making eggs
mcqs.explain: In spermatogenesis the two divisions of meiosis give four equal cells that differentiate into sperm; in oogenesis each division is unequal, producing one large egg with most of the cytoplasm and polar bodies that degenerate.
rationales: A student who applies the 'four cells from meiosis' rule to eggs picks this. In oogenesis the cytoplasm divides unequally, so each meiosis gives one egg and small polar bodies.
A student who generalizes from sperm picks this. All egg-forming cells are made before birth; only spermatogenesis continues producing new gametes throughout adult life.

In spermatogenesis the two divisions of meiosis give four equal cells that differentiate into sperm; in oogenesis each division is unequal, producing one large egg with most of the cytoplasm and polar bodies that degenerate.
A student who assumes the ovulated cell is a finished gamete picks this. The second meiotic division of oogenesis is completed only after a sperm enters the egg.

mcqs.q: A man produces about 100 million sperm per day. A woman is born with about a million egg-forming cells arrested in meiosis, and releases only about 400 eggs in her lifetime. Which conclusion do these figures best support?
options: Eggs are produced continuously like sperm, but nearly all are broken down before they can be ovulated.
Each of the million cells produced four eggs, most of which were not released from the ovary.
The sperm figure must be an overestimate, since fertilization needs only one sperm for each egg.
Egg-forming cells are all made before birth and are then used sparingly over a lifetime.
mcqs.specStatementText: Making sperm and making eggs
mcqs.explain: Oogenesis begins in the foetus with mitosis, growth and the start of meiosis; from puberty a few cells resume meiosis each cycle and one egg is usually released, whereas spermatogenesis produces millions of new sperm daily.
rationales: A student who assumes continuous production picks this. The figures show a fixed stock formed before birth; most of those cells degenerate, but none are newly made after birth.
A student who applies the four-products rule picks this. Each cell that completes meiosis yields one egg plus polar bodies, so four million eggs were never present.
A student who expects gamete numbers to match picks this. Vast sperm numbers are the norm because so few survive the journey to the egg.

Oogenesis begins in the foetus with mitosis, growth and the start of meiosis; from puberty a few cells resume meiosis each cycle and one egg is usually released, whereas spermatogenesis produces millions of new sperm daily.

mcqs.q: In an experiment, eggs treated so that they could not carry out the cortical reaction were each entered by several sperm. Which explanation is correct?
options: Without the cortical reaction the zona pellucida is not hardened, so further sperm can still digest through it and fuse.
The cortical reaction is what lets the first sperm in, so blocking it should have stopped fertilization altogether.
Sperm bore through the egg membrane with their enzymes, so hardening the zona could not have stopped them.
Only one sperm normally reaches the egg, so the treatment must somehow have attracted extra sperm to it.
mcqs.specStatementText: One sperm in, all others out
mcqs.explain: The cortical reaction, triggered by the first sperm's fusion, alters the zona pellucida so that no more sperm can pass through. Blocking it removes the barrier to polyspermy.
rationales: The cortical reaction, triggered by the first sperm's fusion, alters the zona pellucida so that no more sperm can pass through. Blocking it removes the barrier to polyspermy.
A student who has swapped the two reactions picks this. The acrosome reaction lets a sperm through the zona pellucida; the cortical reaction blocks the rest.
A student who thinks enzymes act on the egg membrane picks this. Enzymes digest only the zona pellucida; a hardened zona does stop sperm, which is why the treated eggs let more in.
A student who pictures a single winning sperm picks this. Many sperm reach every egg; what normally stops all but one entering is the cortical reaction.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the blastocyst and implantation is correct?
options: The zygote itself implants in the endometrium immediately after fertilization, before it has divided into a ball of cells.
The blastocyst is a hollow ball with an inner cell mass and implants in the endometrium about a week after fertilization.
The blastocyst is a solid ball of identical cells, every one of which goes on to form part of the foetus.
The blastocyst forms and implants in the uterus, at the same site where fertilization took place.
mcqs.specStatementText: From zygote to blastocyst to implantation
mcqs.explain: By about day 5 to 7 the embryo is a blastocyst: a hollow ball with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that forms the foetus and an outer layer that attaches to and sinks into the endometrium.
rationales: A student who runs fertilization straight into implantation picks this. The zygote divides for several days on its way to the uterus, and only the blastocyst implants.
By about day 5 to 7 the embryo is a blastocyst: a hollow ball with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that forms the foetus and an outer layer that attaches to and sinks into the endometrium.
A student who thinks all the early cells are equivalent picks this. The blastocyst is hollow and its outer layer contributes to the placenta, not the foetus.
A student who places fertilization in the uterus picks this. Fertilization occurs in the oviduct; the blastocyst forms during transit and implants in the endometrium.

mcqs.q: A home pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies. Which statement explains how the test indicates pregnancy?
options: The antibodies bind progesterone, which is present in the urine at a high level only during a pregnancy.
The antibodies bind hCG released into the blood by the mother's pituitary gland when she becomes pregnant.
The antibodies bind hCG in the urine, and only an implanted embryo or its placenta produces hCG.
The woman's own antibodies against hCG appear in her urine and are captured on the test strip.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pregnancy tests detect hCG with monoclonal antibodies
mcqs.explain: Monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG bind it as urine flows along the strip and produce a coloured line; because only the embryo or placenta secretes hCG, its detection indicates pregnancy.
rationales: A student who reaches for the pregnancy hormone picks this. Progesterone is also high in the luteal phase of every cycle; the test detects hCG, which only an embryo makes.
A student who assigns hCG to a maternal gland picks this. hCG is secreted by the embryo and developing placenta, which is why its presence signals pregnancy.
Monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG bind it as urine flows along the strip and produce a coloured line; because only the embryo or placenta secretes hCG, its detection indicates pregnancy.
A student who thinks all antibodies come from the body picks this. The woman does not make antibodies to her own hormone; the strip's monoclonal antibodies are manufactured.

mcqs.q: A foetus in the uterus has fluid-filled, collapsed lungs, yet its blood is oxygenated. How does oxygen reach the blood of the foetus?
options: Maternal blood carrying oxygen flows through the placenta into the blood vessels of the foetus.
The placenta filters oxygen out of the mother's blood while blocking all harmful substances.
The foetus breathes it in from the surrounding amniotic fluid, using its own lungs.
It diffuses from maternal blood into foetal capillaries in the placental villi.
mcqs.specStatementText: The placenta supplies the foetus without mixing bloods
mcqs.explain: Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from maternal blood in the placenta into foetal blood in the capillaries of the villi, whose large surface area makes exchange rapid.
rationales: A student who imagines a shared circulation picks this. Maternal and foetal blood stay separate; oxygen crosses from one to the other in the villi.
A student who sees the placenta as a selective filter picks this. Exchange is by diffusion and transport according to physical properties, and some harmful substances cross.
A student who knows no route to oxygen other than breathing picks this. The foetal lungs are fluid-filled and unused; all gas exchange is across the placenta.
Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from maternal blood in the placenta into foetal blood in the capillaries of the villi, whose large surface area makes exchange rapid.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes the hormonal changes that bring about childbirth?
options: Progesterone falls, contractions begin, and oxytocin rises by positive feedback as the cervix is stretched.
Progesterone rises to a peak that triggers contractions, and oxytocin then falls until the baby is born.
Oxytocin is kept at a steady level by negative feedback so that the contractions stay regular.
The pituitary gland stops secreting progesterone, allowing it to secrete oxytocin in its place.
mcqs.specStatementText: Progesterone keeps pregnancy going; its fall lets birth begin
mcqs.explain: A decrease in progesterone removes the inhibition of uterine contractions and allows oxytocin secretion to increase; stretching of the cervix stimulates more oxytocin release, a positive feedback loop that continues until birth.
rationales: A decrease in progesterone removes the inhibition of uterine contractions and allows oxytocin secretion to increase; stretching of the cervix stimulates more oxytocin release, a positive feedback loop that continues until birth.
A student who expects a rising hormone to trigger the event picks this. Progesterone keeps the uterus relaxed; it is its fall that allows childbirth to start.
A student who assumes all hormonal control is negative feedback picks this. Oxytocin secretion rises progressively by positive feedback during labour.
A student who places progesterone in the pituitary picks this. Progesterone comes from the corpus luteum and then the placenta; the pituitary secretes oxytocin.

mcqs.q: Early epidemiological studies found that women taking HRT had a lower incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD). Later randomized controlled trials found that HRT slightly increased CHD risk. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The early studies were correct because they involved far more women than the trials did, so their result should be preferred.
The correlation was not causal: women on HRT tended to have higher socioeconomic status, which itself lowers CHD risk.
HRT must lower CHD risk in most women, and the trials must have happened to sample an unusual group of women.
The early correlation must have been a chance result: women on HRT did not really have lower CHD rates.
mcqs.specStatementText: HRT and heart disease: correlation is not cause
mcqs.explain: The correlation between HRT and lower CHD was not a cause-and-effect relationship. HRT users had higher socioeconomic status, a factor with a causal relationship to lower CHD risk; the randomized trials showed HRT's own effect is a small increase.
rationales: A student who judges studies by size picks this. However large, an observational study cannot remove differences between women who chose HRT and those who did not; random allocation can.

The correlation between HRT and lower CHD was not a cause-and-effect relationship. HRT users had higher socioeconomic status, a factor with a causal relationship to lower CHD risk; the randomized trials showed HRT's own effect is a small increase.
A student who treats a correlation as proof of cause picks this. The trials were designed to isolate HRT's effect, and they showed a small increase in risk.

A student who thinks a non-causal correlation must be a false finding picks this. The correlation was real and repeatable; what was wrong was the inference that HRT caused the lower rate, when socioeconomic status explained it.

mcqs.q: In a mammal, removing the ovaries (and with them the corpus luteum) early in pregnancy ended the pregnancy, but the same operation late in pregnancy did not. What does this show?
options: The placenta maintained the pregnancy in both cases; the early loss was caused by the stress of surgery.
Later in pregnancy the mother's pituitary gland takes over progesterone secretion, so the ovaries are no longer needed.
Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum at first and later by the placenta once it has formed.
Late in pregnancy the mother's pituitary secretes hCG, which replaced the missing progesterone.
mcqs.specStatementText: Progesterone keeps pregnancy going; its fall lets birth begin
mcqs.explain: Continuity of pregnancy depends on progesterone, secreted initially by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta. Once the placenta has taken over, the ovaries are no longer needed.
rationales: A student who thinks the placenta works from implantation picks this. Early on there is no functioning placenta; the corpus luteum is the only source of the progesterone needed.
A student who places progesterone in the pituitary picks this. Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta; the pituitary secretes FSH, LH and oxytocin, not progesterone.
Continuity of pregnancy depends on progesterone, secreted initially by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta. Once the placenta has taken over, the ovaries are no longer needed.
A student who assigns hCG to a maternal gland picks this. hCG is made by the embryo and placenta, and it is placental progesterone, not hCG, that sustains late pregnancy.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D3.1 Reproduction

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Puberty is treated only as the chain hypothalamus (GnRH) to pituitary (LH and FSH) to gonads (testosterone or oestradiol and progesterone) to the physical changes of puberty. Nothing is included on what causes the rise in GnRH release (no leptin, kisspeptin or body-mass triggers), on pulsatile secretion, or on the individual secondary sexual characteristics beyond naming them as the changes of puberty.

The only named stages are zygote and blastocyst. The terms morula, gastrula, gastrulation, germ layers, embryonic disc and cleavage stage counts (2-cell, 8-cell) are not used anywhere in the bank; the blastocyst is described only as a hollow ball with an inner cell mass and an outer layer of cells that attaches to the endometrium.

The placenta is described only in terms of villi projecting into maternal blood, their large surface area, the exchange processes across them and the retention of the foetus to a later stage. No item names chorion, intervillous spaces, umbilical vessels, syncytiotrophoblast, the barrier layers or the number of cell layers between the two circulations.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
